prospects.thesis: RTX is the highest composite score on the screen and offers diversified exposure across Pratt & Whitney (commercial aero recovery), Raytheon (missiles/air defense), and Collins Aerospace — a rare three-legged stool benefiting from both the defense upcycle and commercial aerospace rebound. Bullish options flow combined with bullish institutional positioning signals smart money accumulation ahead of continued DoD budget tailwinds and Golden Dome/missile defense spending. At $266B cap with reasonable 2.8x P/S, it's the quality anchor for a defense allocation.

LMT is breaking out with +17.9% 1M momentum as F-35 production stabilizes and missile segment (PAC-3, THAAD, Javelin) sees surging international demand from Europe, Israel, and Indo-Pacific allies. Bullish institutional flow and a reasonable 1.7x P/S for a prime contractor with multi-decade backlog visibility makes this a core defense holding distinct from RTX's commercial exposure. The pullback in yields is an added tailwind for long-duration defense cash flows.

HII is the sole US builder of nuclear-powered aircraft carriers and one of two submarine builders — a near-impenetrable moat as AUKUS submarine production and Columbia/Virginia-class demand accelerates. +14.9% 1M momentum with bullish institutional positioning signals the market is finally rewarding the naval shipbuilding super-cycle thesis. Cheap at 0.9x P/S with a differentiated sub-niche (naval) that doesn't overlap with RTX or LMT.

MSFT remains the most monetizable AI platform play through Azure OpenAI, Copilot across Office/GitHub, and enterprise AI infrastructure — with bullish options flow and institutional accumulation reinforcing the setup. At $4.14T cap it provides mega-cap AI exposure that diversifies the watchlist's defense tilt, and the falling 10Y yield (-6bps WoW) is supportive for long-duration tech. Next catalysts: Azure growth re-acceleration and Copilot attach rate disclosures.

SAIC occupies the defense IT services sub-niche (distinct from prime contractors and shipbuilders), providing software, digital engineering, and systems integration to DoD and intelligence community customers — directly leveraged to DoD's software modernization and AI-enablement push. +19.1% 1M momentum with bullish institutional flow and a very cheap 0.9x P/S offers asymmetric value versus the primes. Small-cap ($6.3B) adds torque to the defense theme.

market_pulse.rotation_analysis: The smart money is piling into Financials, Communication Services, and quietly into Utilities — a classic "barbell" setup where big players want banks to benefit from a steeper yield curve and ongoing deregulation chatter (the administration has been openly friendly to bank M&A and capital rule rollbacks), while simultaneously grabbing defensive yield in Utilities as a hedge. Meanwhile, options traders are aggressively betting against Energy, Materials, Industrials, and Healthcare — Energy's 11.7x volume with a 2.94 put/call is a screaming signal someone thinks oil demand or prices are rolling over, likely tied to tariff-driven global growth fears and the administration's "drill baby drill" supply push, while Healthcare puts are stacking up ahead of drug pricing executive orders and Medicare negotiation expansions that Washington keeps teasing. The Tech bearishness is the eyebrow-raiser — despite the AI narrative driving headlines, the options market is betting big on a pullback, probably because export controls on chips to China are tightening and valuations are stretched going into earnings. The real tell is the credit market: investment-grade bonds (LQD) are getting bid while junk bonds (HYG) are getting dumped and spreads are widening, which historically front-runs an economic slowdown by 1-3 months — meaning the "rotation into Financials" might actually be a short-term deregulation trade inside a broader defensive pivot. The non-obvious inference nobody's talking about: when you see Staples AND Utilities getting bought while Industrials and Materials get sold, that's not a rotation, that's institutions quietly preparing for a growth scare — possibly because tariff implementation timelines are about to hit real earnings, and the bond market is already sniffing it out before equities catch on.
